extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers (PIs, postdocs, grad students), grant applicants, peer reviewers, and those engaged with NIH extramural funding and academic career issues
extracted.subtask_description: Opinionated blog guidance on academic careers, NIH funding behavior, peer review practices, and institutional responses to sexual harassment — aimed at researchers and grant applicants thinking about strategy, ethics, and professional conduct. Covers practical advice for submitting grants, suggesting reviewers, publishing funded work, and influencing change inside vs outside institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide to quit if you don't like the job
rubrics_metrics.description: If you don't like the job, why on earth are you still doing it? (friend's advice recalled during dissertation struggles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether you genuinely like the work; if you persist only out of inertia or sunk-cost thinking, consider leaving to pursue something more interesting or fulfilling. The post frames this as a sanity check rather than a formal rule — ask yourself whether continuing is worth the personal cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance — grind it out when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: I had to grit my teeth and grind out my dissertation year... Grind, my friends. Grind it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some intervals (dissertation writing, difficult project phases) require sustained effort and endurance. Practical implication: be prepared for periods of low enjoyment but necessary completion; balance this with the previous criterion about deciding whether to continue in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest equal numbers of female and male reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Commit yourself to suggest at least as many female reviewers as you do male ones for each and every one of your manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a corresponding author (or any author), make a default practice of nominating at least as many women as men as potential reviewers; if needed, include postdocs. Rationale: data showed only 25–34% of suggested reviewers were women; author action is a simple, immediate step to improve gender balance in peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of gendered reviewer exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Women corresponding authors nominate female peers to exclude at twice the rate of male corresponding authors (lower pie charts observation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation uncertain (could reflect women seeing more women as peers), but be aware that exclusion suggestions can have gendered patterns. When listing excluded reviewers, consider whether exclusions are justified or contribute to bias and reduced representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit proposals that meet minimal standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Always submit something that hits the minimal standards for a reviewer to get behind it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are going to submit, ensure the application is credible and satisfies baseline expectations so it avoids triage. The author’s mantra: better to submit a proposal that reaches minimal acceptability than a weak one destined to be screened out. Practical: vet methodologic rigor, clarity of aims, and fit to the FOA before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply to highly targeted RFAs only if you are the right person and will pursue the stated approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Targeted FOAs (e.g., for 'Approach X') should be applied to by investigators actually capable and intending to carry out that approach — funding recipients should work on the work the grant solicited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an FOA explicitly targets a specific approach, grantees ought to pursue that approach rather than diverting to other lines (Approach Y). The author criticizes labs that receive focused funding and then publish little or unrelated work, noting it is unfair to applicants who declined to apply because they lacked funding. Practical implication: ensure alignment between proposal, capabilities, and planned outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to publish results from grant-funded work
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have been paid to work on the project, there is an obligation to produce on that project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PIs bear a heavy responsibility to write up and publish datasets generated with grant dollars, even if trainees have left; publishing old or negative results is part of the ethical bargain of being funded. The author notes practical obstacles (staff departure) but insists on PI accountability to produce published science for grant dollars awarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insider and outsider strategies both matter for systemic change
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it more effective to drive change from inside the room or from outside the room? The author argues we need both approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work inside institutions (e.g., serving on study section, influencing Program Officers) to push change via sober, diplomatic efforts, while also using outside channels (blogging, public critique) to keep pressure and visibility on issues. Balance tone and tactics: choose when to be 'shouty' and when to be 'sober' depending on context and potential efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate your behavior on study sections; choose when to speak
rubrics_metrics.description: When on study section I have to moderate my behavior. When do I speak up and what do I say?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an insider reviewer, weigh the potential impact of comments and interventions; sometimes oblique mentions (e.g., of bias reports like Ginther) can nudge others, while overt shouting may be counterproductive. Tactical consideration: maximize influence by calibrating interventions to the setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior faculty should consider stepping aside to open jobs
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminating mandatory retirement reduced the number of new assistant professor slots (example: MIT saw a 19% reduction in new slots). Senior faculty staying in place can block career opportunities for younger scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the structural impact of prolonged senior faculty careers on hiring; consider career transitions (e.g., emeritus, partial-retirement positions) that responsibly open opportunities for junior scholars. The author frames this as both an institutional and ethical consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional societies and journals must adopt policies to address sexual harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic societies often lack mechanisms to remove members found to have engaged in sexual harassment; journals sometimes publish defenses of proven harassers — both are harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for societies to implement clear removal and sanction policies, and for journals/editors to avoid publishing defenses of individuals proven to have engaged in harassment. Support grassroots efforts like MeTooSTEM (e.g., fundraising to become nonprofit) to provide resources to victims and to pressure institutions to change.
